data.description: An operator using Chinese-language instructions reportedly directed Cairn, an AI agent framework, to breach more than 100 company websites. The campaign targeted sites in the U.S., Canada, Australia, and Japan. Researchers verified unauthorized access tools on victim servers. Reuters identified websites belonging to farm equipment maker Deere and appliance maker SharkNinja; the extent of data theft remained unclear.

reports.title: How one hacker used AI agents and a few thousand dollars to break into scores of sites
Inside Cairn: Open Windows into massive AI-Driven Cyber Operations

reports_full.text:
WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Over the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched as a Chinese-speaking hacker broke into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere [(DE.N)](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/DE.N), home appliance ​company SharkNinja [(SN.N)](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/SN.N) and engine manufacturer Cummins [(CMI.N)](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/CMI.N).

Yet the hacker did almost none of the work.

The cybercriminal instead outsourced the hacking spree almost entirely to artificial intelligence, tasking AI agents ‌with spending hours autonomously probing and breaking into targeted sites, according to Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge.

In a report provided to Reuters ahead of [publication on Monday](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn), Fagerland said the hacker was one of several he discovered while scanning the web for inadvertently exposed instances of Cairn, an open-source AI problem-solving platform popular with hackers. Beginning around October 2, Fagerland said he found about two dozen instances of Cairn being used for malicious activity, which allowed him ​to quietly peer over the cybercriminals' shoulders as they set their AI tools loose on the world.

Fagerland's report on the Chinese-speaking hacker did not name the victims, but Reuters was able ​to establish the victims' identities by independently reviewing the hacker's Cairn activity.

At a time of [rising anxiety](https://www.reuters.com/business/what-amodei-altman-musk-have-said-about-ai-risks-stoking-doom-fears-2026-10-14/) over the power of autonomous AI tools, Fagerland said ⁠his find was real-life evidence that commercially available AI agents could pull off complex intrusions from start to finish without human intervention, a dramatic boost to the power of a single malicious actor.

"It's ​a new world now," said Fagerland.

Reuters could not ascertain the degree to which the breaches resulted in unauthorized extraction of data.

Deere told Reuters it had taken "necessary remediation actions" following the incident and had "no indication that ​sensitive information was accessed." SharkNinja said the hack had hit a standalone site carrying only product support information and that the threat had been contained. Cummins said it was "investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors."

Two smaller businesses also acknowledged being compromised. Other victims listed in the Cairn data did not return messages.

## FEW INSTRUCTIONS, MANY HACKS

One of the hackers that Fagerland observed stole a trove of credit card data. Another ​tried to get AI agents to rob a cryptocurrency exchange. The Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific. Beginning on September 25, they set their AI army loose against US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese ​e-commerce websites.

Their instructions were terse, sketching out their preferred intrusion tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters. As of late last week, their agents had attempted to break into more than 1,200 sites. Successful intrusions typically took around ‌23 hours ⁠of poking and prodding for vulnerabilities. Fagerland estimated that the campaign, which appeared to be using a mixture of China's DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code, had chewed up roughly $5,000 worth of tokens, or about $50 per successful hack.

Fagerland — who has worked in cybersecurity for nearly three decades — said he was impressed by some of the techniques the agents used to compromise their victims. In one case, after failing to find any weaknesses in a big company's public-facing application, the AI agents pored through digital records to find associated infrastructure, located a public-facing control panel, discovered a subtle weakness in the way it processed data, and after ​hours of trial and error, reported leveraging it ​to trick the server into executing malicious commands.

"It's ⁠not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland said. "It's not script kiddie stuff."

Cairn's author, whose social media handle is "le1xia0", acknowledged receipt of a Reuters message but did not immediately answer a list of questions. In a recent post on X, they said their platform was "an innovative type of multi-agent architecture and was ​not designed for hacking attacks. If it is used to carry out harmful hacking attacks, that is not my intention."

## NO SUPERVISION NEEDED

The ability of ​agentic AI systems to autonomously ⁠discover vulnerabilities, conduct intrusions, and steal data is a source of increasing anxiety around the world. Rogue agents inadvertently unleashed by major AI companies have [hacked their way out of computer labs](https://www.reuters.com/world/openai-works-understand-full-scope-agent-activity-user-data-leak-emerges-2026-09-25/) [,](https://www.reuters.com/world/openai-works-understand-full-scope-agent-activity-user-data-leak-emerges-2026-09-25/) [broken into government websites](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/australia-steps-up-response-ai-after-openai-bot-breaches-health-system-database-2026-09-25/), and engaged in [unsanctioned social engineering attempts](https://www.reuters.com/world/how-texas-student-blew-whistle-rogue-ai-hacking-attempt-2026-08-20/). South Korea and Japan have in recent weeks been buffeted by a series of well-publicized hacks attributed to [AI-using cybercriminals](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/south-korea-japan-buffeted-by-hacks-ai-lowers-bar-cybercriminals-2026-10-09/).

AI agents are increasingly becoming staples of the cybercriminal underground. In August, the Israeli firm ⁠Gambit Security found ​that Russian-speaking extortionists had [leveraged SpaceX's Cursor AI tool](https://www.reuters.com/world/russian-speaking-cybercriminals-used-spacexs-cursor-ai-tool-hack-seven-companies-2026-08-27/) to break into seven organizations. In September, Gambit documented [an AI agent-driven spree](https://gambit.security/blog-posts/autonomous-ai-agents-online-retailers-25-a-company) ​that resulted in breaches at 25 companies and the theft of at least 600,000 credit card records. Last week, the cyber intelligence company Bitsight said that discussions about how to use autonomous agents were [surging across cybercriminal forums](https://www.bitsight.com/blog/evolution-of-ai-cybercrime-underground-forums).

Fagerland said he had previously assumed ​hacker-agents would need at least some supervision. He said it was now obvious that the technology had moved past that.

"The development in this field is astounding," he said.

Reporting by Raphael Satter; Editing by Rosalba O'Brien
reports_full.title: How one hacker used AI agents and a few thousand dollars to break into scores of sites

reports_full.text:
More than 20 exposed Cairn panels give an unusually detailed view of how threat actors select targets, direct autonomous agents, exploit vulnerabilities, and establish persistent access to compromised systems.

## 01 TL;DR

An investigation by NorForge into publicly exposed AI-driven penetration-testing control panels has uncovered how they are extensively used in malicious cyber operations. One of these is Cairn.

In this setting, Cairn is an AI-powered hacking system. Give it a target and an objective, and it can coordinate AI agents to investigate the target, search for security weaknesses, and attempt to break in.

More than 20 exposed Cairn panels were identified as likely associated with malicious activity, providing an unusually detailed view of how threat actors select targets, direct autonomous agents, exploit vulnerabilities, and establish persistent access to compromised systems.

In addition, a considerable number of apparently legitimate red team operations were also exposed this way, potentially placing clients at risk.

## 02 The Opening

In September 2026, Gambit Security reported on a criminal intrusion campaign targeting online marketplaces. They recovered an attacker’s staging server and found the use of AI harnesses, such as Hermes, Strix, and Cairn. Important information, that is. Such tools frequently have web based user interfaces that are left unsecured on the open web.

Sure enough: Quick searches using the Shodan and Censys search engines reveal hosts running what appear to be AI harnesses of different kinds. Most need authorization to access. Most.

But there are quite a few of these interfaces left open by their operators. And apparently, one of the most neglected platforms is Cairn.

Our searches initially revealed a handful of open Cairn panels. Continued scans revealed new panels coming online in short order; and targeting information, language and instructions showed many of them to belong to the same threat actors.

In this article we will detail some of these. However; it is the nature of these panels that they reveal a great deal of sensitive information about the targets; including who they are, what weaknesses have been uncovered, account secrets and API keys, and whether they have been compromised or not. This means that we must aggressively redact extracted data and won’t disclose the panel addresses until they can be taken down.

[![An operator task on an open Cairn panel, with target names and credentials redacted.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/operator-task-secrets.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/operator-task-secrets.webp)

*Operator task containing secrets. Even root access to the attacker’s data drop is exposed.*

## 03 The Machine

[![A Cairn panel listing active and completed projects.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/cairn-panel-projects.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/cairn-panel-projects.webp)

*A Cairn panel with a few active or completed projects. This belongs to an unrelated actor; conveniently not using recognizable target tags.*

Some describe Cairn as an autonomous penetration testing engine. This is not entirely accurate; it can be used that way, yes, but its use case is more generic: It is a state-based problem solving engine, moving step by step in the general direction of a defined solution.

But in our case – yes, it is used for penetration testing.

In Cairn, each separate task is considered a project. Every project has a start point called an origin, and a predefined end goal. The agent framework then progresses from origin towards goal in a state-based organic growth.

Between start and end are cycles of intents and facts. A fact is something the agent has discovered, and an intent is what it has decided to do next. The agent posts every fact onto a project-internal blackboard. A human operator can also add their own hints to the same blackboard. Facts and hints are in this way data available to every agent worker on the path towards the defined solution. This can be visualized graphically, which also Cairn does.

[![A Cairn project graph running from origin to goal.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/project-graph.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/project-graph.webp)

*The progress from origin in cyan to goal in red. Not all paths succeed. This attack was directed at a major US online retailer, and ended up in GOAL MET: Webshell injected into the site.*

## 04 The Actors

Cairn panels are regular web fronts, and can be readily profiled using commercial internet scanning platforms. Over a period of a few days, we found numerous such panels. Some were empty, some were protected against unauthorized access, and some appeared to be legitimate demos or valid pentesting outfits. We will not be outing legitimate red teams here, but it is clear that placing real customer penetration tests on an unsecured panel is highly problematic.

But even filtering out those, more than 20 such panels were identified as likely malicious. As far as we could see, all appeared to have financial motivation; there was no obvious state-sponsored intrusion activity. That is not to say that this does not happen, but one assumes that type of actor knows how to secure dashboards.

Much of the observed activity seemed to coalesce around a handful of clusters, where the exposed panels contained information that tied them together.

We denote each activity cluster by a serial number starting with the “AIA” prefix; meaning “AI Activity”. The acronym for AI Threat Activity was already taken.

### Cluster AIA0001

- **Language**  
  Chinese
- **Panels**  
  14
- **Hosting**  
  AS56594
- **Confidence**  
  High

This activity cluster uses Chinese language, and is by far the most active of the actors that expose their panels. The operation is massive, with over 1100 attack projects spread over the 14 dashboards likely associated with this group.

AIA0001 targets a wide swath of organizations, mostly in the US, Japan and Australia. The aim seems to be to gain persistent access to e-commerce/payment infrastructure for later monetization.

This group currently seems to prefer hosting their panels via AS56594, Cgi Global Limited. We assess this cluster to be malicious with high confidence.

[![Bar chart of AIA0001 targets by sector.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/aia0001-target-selection.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/aia0001-target-selection-2400w.webp)

*AIA0001 target selection.*

This actor appears to use extensive automation in its task feeding pipeline. Consider for example this task, which is quite typical:

[![A typical automated AIA0001 task, written in Chinese.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/aia0001-automated-task.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/aia0001-automated-task.webp)

*A typical automated task.*

> **Translation**
>
> These are confirmed real shopping/e-commerce websites in four countries (US/CA/JP/AU), with traffic of 200,000–1.5 million. Playwright has verified that orders can be placed.
>
> Objective: Find unauthenticated RCE (command execution/code injection/deserialization/file-upload webshell/SQL injection leading to RCE/SSTI/SSRF leading to RCE).
>
> Priorities: Login SQL injection, unauthenticated endpoints, file uploads, deserialization, authentication bypass, account takeover.
>
> Payload: Uploader shell (HTML upload form + move\_uploaded\_file to save files), explicitly not a command-executing webshell.

The feeding pipeline includes automated validation of target sites. Not only are they ranked by traffic, but they have also been tested using Playwright, Microsoft’s browser automation framework, before sent to Cairn for exploitation.

There are also other hints at automation; and some are of the silly kind. For example; a lot of target sites across multiple panels have had an initial letter “w” removed. ‘Wholesale’ becomes ‘holesale’ and “winter” becomes “inter”. This suggests that there is a common, buggy domain normalizer that removes a “w” too much from the www. It makes spotting related panels very easy.

Every now and then, these attackers will open a web server on a high port to do out of band testing. In these short lived time windows, the working directory of one of these AI workers will be available for browsing. This happened at least once with one of the AIA0001 hosts, and that gave us the opportunity to get a closer look at the tooling available for the agent.

In this particular case, we found:

*Tools found on agent worker folder*

| Software / package / tool | Use case |
| --- | --- |
| Playwright | Browser automation and web testing; the profile directories are Chromium browser state rather than source packages. |
| Chromium | Browser engine used by Playwright and related browser automation. |
| PHPGGC (PHP Generic Gadget Chains) | Generates PHP unserialize() gadget-chain payloads for authorized vulnerability validation and exploit research. |
| StyleSmuggler HTTP PoC | Research proof-of-concept for the StyleSmuggler / CVE-2026-75650 Magento report-poisoning-to-code-execution chain. |
| Magento Open Source 2.4.9 validation lab | Docker-based, revision-pinned vulnerable/patched Magento lab for safely validating CVE-2026-75650 / VULN-39341. |
| MarkShust PolyShellPatch | Deprecated Magento module intended to block executable-file uploads through cart custom-option uploads. |
| Docker | Container build/runtime tooling used for isolated validation environments. |
| PHP | Runtime and scripting language for PHP payload generation and testing PHP web applications. |
| Composer | PHP dependency/package manager; the manifest identifies the Magento PolyShellPatch package. |
| Python 3 | Main scripting language for reconnaissance, HTTP testing, parsers, proof-of-concept code, and automation. |
| Node.js | JavaScript runtime/tooling used by web probes, browser automation support, and target-specific scripts. |
| Vosk | Offline speech-recognition toolkit/model. |
| OpenSSL | TLS/cryptographic command-line and configuration tooling. |
| Xvfb | X virtual framebuffer for running GUI/browser applications without a physical display. |
| tmux | Terminal multiplexer/runtime state, typically used to keep long-running sessions and listeners alive. |
| OWASP Amass | External attack-surface discovery and subdomain enumeration. |
| dnsrecon | DNS enumeration and reconnaissance. |
| ffuf | Fast web fuzzer for directory, parameter, virtual-host, and content discovery. |
| Nmap | Network/port/service scanning. |
| rockyou wordlist | Large password wordlist commonly used for authorized password-audit and credential-testing workflows. |
| Odoo framework artifacts | Extracted Odoo server/module source or probes used to understand Odoo web, ORM, QWeb, and action execution behavior. |
| Various custom utilities | Project-specific proxying, payload validation, traffic capture, patching, and proof-of-concept utilities. |

But more importantly, one of the agent task updates contained this text:

> **Agent task update**
>
> The local environment is a Kali container, belonging to the tsec CTF/intelligent penetration test competition framework (there is a flag submission interface description in `/home/kali/workspace/.claude/skills/tsec-actions/SKILL.md`, with the flag format being `flag{...}`), but the environment variable `TSEC_SERVER_HOST` is empty and `TSEC_AGENT_TOKEN` is not actually injected, so the competition submission interface cannot be accessed

This would seem to indicate that the agent setup was repurposed from an earlier Tencent CTF challenge configuration. This is almost certainly criminals reusing existing tools, and there is no reason to believe that Tencent had anything to do with this operation.

From what we’ve seen, all tasks were performed by a worker named `claudecode_deepseek-v4.1-flash`, which could mean a Claude Code harness using the Chinese DeepSeek 4.1 Flash model that was released in September.

We dont have actual numbers on token usage, but with the underlying data it's possible to guesstimate. Deepseek 4.1 Flash is an inexpensive model, but cost varies between peak and non-peak hours, and whether the tokens are cached or not. We estimate the average cost of a task to end up around $5 if one includes unsuccessful, early ending projects. Longer running projects could get more expensive - there are projects with over 1000 intents and facts, and those could end up costing more than $100. The uncertainty here is however considerable, and numbers could be off by a clear margin. Even so, there's no doubt that this is relatively cheap.

### Cluster AIA0002

- **Language**  
  English
- **Panels**  
  10
- **Hosting**  
  AS20473
- **Confidence**  
  High

This cluster uses English language, and is oriented towards financial theft. We found 10 panels likely associated with this group, though some of these are less confidently linked. Many of these have also gone dark since the start of this investigation.

They frequently directly talk about stealing credit cards and cryptocurrencies, and uploading stolen data to separate hosts under their control. They – incredibly! – expose the SSH login to backend staging hosts in their taskings. (No, we did not log into their servers, although we were sorely tempted.) It is interesting to see that many projects seem to have no technical starting instructions, beyond "fetch credit cards" or "fetch crypto". The agents just go from there.

This group prefer hosting their panels via AS20473, The Constant Company (in most cases this means VULTR VPS instances). We assess this cluster to be malicious with high confidence.

The targets listed in these panels are mainly oriented towards merchant payment services, gray-market payment sites and pharmaceutical sites; even a clearly criminal carding site. There are indications that they successfully breached some of these.

Out of the targets that do not fit into those categories, several are African commerce sites, which hints towards this actor having a base on that continent.

[![Bar chart of AIA0002 targets by sector.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/aia0002-target-sectors.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/aia0002-target-sectors-2400w.webp)

*AIA0002 target sectors.*

The projects run by this actor state they use workers named pi\_openrouter\_deepseek, suggesting a configuration in which the Pi coding-agent framework uses DeepSeek language models through OpenRouter, a third-party AI model API gateway.

### Cluster AIA0003

- **Language**  
  English
- **Panels**  
  1
- **Hosting**  
  AS200019
- **Confidence**  
  Low

This entity exposes only one panel, with 59 projects listed. The targets are a mix of smaller e-commerce sites and very large US-based commercial platforms. Language used is exclusively English. The panel is hosted on AS200019, AlexHost.

The projects listed on this panel start out claiming to be authorized assessments of various sites, but then gradually become more explicit about exploiting the targets including obtaining shell access, admin panel access, or database access.

This actor seems more in the exploratory stage. We assess this actor to be malicious with low confidence.

[![Dashboard of project creation over time for AIA0001, AIA0002 and AIA0003.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/project-creation-activity.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/project-creation-activity.webp)

*Project creation activity across the three clusters.*

## 05 The Exploitation

Whether a task has succeeded in reaching its goal, and whether that constitutes a real-life security problem, depends a lot on how aggressive a goal is. In some cases, tasks stop when establishing whether there is a vulnerability. However, the threat actors covered in this article typically go further.

Previously, we posted one of the tasks used by AIA0001. That task explicitly demanded a webshell to be installed, in order for the goal to be reached. Just to test, we checked if one of the claimed intrusions had really happened by fetching the shell URL mentioned in a completed task against a large hardware parts vendor. The URL did indeed serve an uploader webshell. Attackers can at any time change that into something more malicious.

[![A bare file-upload form served from the vendor's site.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/live-uploader-webshell.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/live-uploader-webshell.webp)

*Live uploader web shell served from a vendor site.*

This particular intrusion was apparently – according to the agent’s own explanation – enabled by unauthorized write access to a memcached session store, combined with unsafe PHP object deserialization and an exploitable gadget chain in legacy Zend Framework components. However, all these exploitation paths are different, and the payload can look different as well. We have gathered a number of case studies at the end of this paper.

AIA0001 seems to exclusively go after access, and make sure they have the ability to do more at a later date. Other actors have other goals, but this threat actor appears to have been by far the most proficient and effective in reaching their target. The AIA0002 actor uses Cairn in a more generic way. Not only is it used to break into targets, but it is also used as a general purpose service engine; for example to move funds between crypto wallets.

*Task types*

| Activity | Typical task goals (literal quotes) |
| --- | --- |
| AIA0001 | 这是四国(US/CA/JP/AU)已确认的真实购物电商站(流量200k-1.5M)。 |

| AIA0003 | Obtain shell access, admin panel access, or database access on REDACTED. Try all attack vectors: SQLi, file upload, authentication bypass, RCE, deserialization, SSTI, SSRF, business logic flaws. Build dynamic attack chains. |

## 06 The Success Rates

The different activity clusters have different focus, go after different targets, and what constitutes success varies. They are not directly comparable. But it is a reasonable assumption that for the harnesses we have seen in these campaigns, average success rate is hovering around 10%, with many of the remaining tasks achieving partial goals, or are able to gather information that can be used in later attempts.

- **Average success rate**  
  ~10%
- **Start to goal, AIA0001**  
  <23h
- **Facts per project**  
  140

[![Summary of observed AI-driven intrusion campaigns and their reported outcomes.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/campaign-outcomes.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/campaign-outcomes.webp)

*Observed AI-driven intrusion campaigns and reported outcomes.*

If we concentrate on the tasks that did reach their goals, especially on the AIA0001 cluster which most resembles general purpose intrusion activity, we can now see that the average time from project start to goal met was a little under 23 hours, generating on average 140 facts per project. However; there’s a wide range here. One project ran for more than five days. It is also worth noting that this is a snapshot at this point in time. Models and harnesses evolve very quickly.

## 07 The Exposure

These panels not only expose that a site is being tested for weaknesses, and any conclusions of the tests. They detail everything that the agent has discovered in the process, and if that was not enough, they include human input that includes credentials harvested elsewhere.

In other words, having your site tested on an open Cairn instance is often a serious security issue, regardless of outcome of the test.

We ran the secrets scanner Trufflehog over the data from these Cairn instances.

[![Dashboard of credentials found in exposed Cairn project data, by risk, verification status and secret type.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/exposed-credentials.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/exposed-credentials-2400w.webp)

*Credentials exposed in AI-driven operations.*

The result was concerning. Literally hundreds of secrets of different kinds, from relatively trivial to extremely serious; with 11% verified valid by Trufflehog.

Think that's bad? It gets worse. These panels appear completely unprotected, exposing what looks like the full administrative functionality of the harness. That includes controls for starting and stopping projects, interfering with ongoing operations, inserting new data, redirecting agents to different targets, and restarting old projects. We haven't tested whether these controls actually work without authorization, for reasons that should be fairly obvious. But consider the implications. These are autonomous offensive agents with considerable capabilities, potentially available to anyone who stumbles across their control panels. Tokens could evaporate like dry ice on a hot plate. And who knows what these agents could be persuaded to do that would make their owners weep. Just to be clear, we walked away from that train of thought. But the underlying point remains: Whatever offensive expertise these operators possess, securing their own infrastructure does not appear to be among their strengths.

## 08 The Conclusion

It is clear that AI-driven frameworks are used to perform malicious actions. That was established well before this paper. However, this research has pointed out something else: The attackers are not well prepared for this technology either. In the rush to gain quick results, many have forgotten basic security precautions, leading to them compromising their own operational security and also, unfortunately, exposing their targets to a far larger attack surface than the intent was. This has also proven to be a problem for legitimate red teams; gathering secrets from your client just to publish them on the Internet is a nightmare scenario.

But it is an interesting window into the methodology, and how autonomous and semi-autonomous agents solve real world intrusion tasks. This could and should inform our defenses going forward.

We have been cooperating with Reuters in notifying victims, particularly those who appear to have suffered a compromise. We are also attempting to get the offending Cairn panels taken down. This might not be possible; it depends a lot on how well the hosters respond to takedown requests.

## A Case studies

### Case 1 Australian e-commerce site

The Cairn backend stated that goal was met and indeed, there is a shell giving command execution on the web server.

[![A directory listing returned by a web shell on the site, with identifying details redacted.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case1-command-shell.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case1-command-shell.webp)

*Command execution through the shell on the web server.*

[![Attack chain from unauthenticated account modification to server command execution.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case1-attack-chain.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case1-attack-chain.webp)

*The attack chain, from unauthenticated account modification to command execution.*

### Case 2 Restaurant POS compromise

[![Attack chain of the restaurant POS compromise.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case2-restaurant-pos.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case2-restaurant-pos.webp)

*Restaurant POS compromise.*

### Case 3 Web application intrusion on US retailer

[![Attack chain of the web application intrusion on a US retailer.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case3-us-retailer.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case3-us-retailer.webp)

*US retailer web application intrusion.*

### Case 4 Another US retailer, this time via insecure error handling

[![Attack chain through insecure error handling at a US retailer.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case4-error-handling.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case4-error-handling.webp)

*Insecure error handling.*

### Case 5 Japanese retailer

[![Attack chain of the intrusion on a Japanese retailer.](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case5-japanese-retailer.webp)](https://norforge.com/blog/inside_cairn/images/case5-japanese-retailer.webp)

reports_full.text:
An Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police.

The AI reportedly submitted this incorrect information to a public Philadelphia Police Department (PPD) tip line on July 18, but Anthropic didn't discover the behavior until September 28. The police had not seen the tip because it was marked as spam.

Anthropic notified the PPD about the incident on Wednesday and met with the department the following day.

"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable," the PPD said in a statement to [6abc](https://6abc.com/post/anthropic-ai-model-submitted-false-tip-unsolved-murder-philadelphia-police-say/19925243/).

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but the PPD elaborated on the incident in an emailed press release shared with TechCrunch.

"According to Anthropic, its model was conducting a test involving interactions with randomly selected websites when it accessed PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com and submitted false information concerning an unsolved homicide. The submission, dated July 18, 2026, at 11:27 p.m., purported to come from someone who might have information about the case," the PPD said.

As autonomous [AI agents](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/03/all-the-ai-agents-that-can-live-in-your-text-messages/) are increasingly made available to consumers, this incident highlights the danger of giving AI the ability to carry out tasks without any human supervision.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been especially vocal about his belief that AI development should be slowed down so that labs can implement adequate guardrails. Perhaps this stance was informed, in part, by witnessing his company's tools submit false homicide tips.

These issues are not exclusive to Anthropic. OpenAI recently revealed that one of its models acted unexpectedly during a test and [hacked the AI dataset platform Hugging Face](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/22/how-an-openais-human-mistake-led-to-the-ai-powered-hack-on-hugging-face/), exposing critical vulnerabilities in its software. As AI models continue to be granted unchecked access to people's computers and login credentials, this problem is expected to persist.

"Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers," the PPD added. "Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement."

Anthropic subsequently published [a blog post](https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions) acknowledging the false tip as part of a larger pattern of its models behaving in unintended ways. In response, the company said it will [cut off its internal evaluations from the live internet](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/anthropic-cant-reliably-control-its-ai-agents-its-cutting-off-its-internal-evals-from-the-live-internet-instead/).

*This article has been updated with information from Anthropic's blog post.*

reports_full.text:
This report describes examples of unintended model actions we've observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude. It is part of our effort to publish more frequent standalone reports on model behavior and alignment beyond our system cards, which we publish with each model release, and our risk reports, which we publish every three to six months as part of our Responsible Scaling Policy. We believe it's important to be transparent about what we see our models do during testing and use.

The behaviors can be grouped into four categories:

-   Claude exploiting a basic flaw in software to run commands on a server;
-   Claude submitting a sensitive form on a real website when it should not have;
-   Claude working around a restriction to reach data that was gated by a token or a fee; and
-   Claude using URL shortening services to get around limits in its fetch tool.

We have chosen not to name the organizations involved in the examples below to avoid exposing vulnerabilities in their systems, and at their request. For this reason, we also provide less detail about each case than we otherwise would. Some of the cases described below involved websites run by U.S. government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels. We have briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved.

The cases we've identified to date in these categories had minimal real-world impact. We consider these behaviors to be significantly less severe from an alignment and security perspective than the cybersecurity incidents we reported on [July 30](https://www.anthropic.com/news/investigating-incidents-cybersecurity-evals) and [September 9](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents). They resemble behaviors that we've described in our system cards since [Claude Mythos Preview](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/08ab9158070959f88f296514c21b7facce6f52bc.pdf). Most are forms of *persistence*, in which Claude, when it cannot complete a task as given, works around a restriction instead of stopping.

Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures (described in the remediation section of this post) reliably catch behaviors like these. Below, we also discuss alignment considerations and give more detail on how we're modifying training to reduce the likelihood of further misbehavior.

We identified most of these cases through a review of transcripts that we began in July. Our review first focused on our cybersecurity evaluations---tests where a model is deliberately asked to probe or attack a test system, and where internet access is meant to be disabled. We have since extended our scanning to encompass a much wider range of instances where Claude could have reached the internet, including tests where internet access is deliberately enabled so Claude can be evaluated on real-world tasks. We began by looking for incidents of similar severity to the cybersecurity incidents we reported this summer; we have not found any to date. We then broadened the search to lower-severity cases, where a model interacted with real websites or systems in ways we didn't intend.

We are also now scanning a much larger pool of lower-risk transcripts, as well as our use of Claude within Anthropic and in reinforcement learning (RL) environments where Claude has access to the internet. As this work continues, we plan to report new instances of unintended behaviors. All cases reported here involved Claude interacting with the outside world; to our knowledge, none of them involved customer data or Anthropic's own internal systems.

In this post, we explain why we run evaluations, which are where most of these cases occurred; describe each behavior in more detail; and offer a preliminary view of what the behaviors suggest about Claude's alignment and how we're mitigating them.

Why and how we run evaluations
------------------------------

The behaviors described in this post are not specific to evaluations, but many of the cases we've identified to date occurred during evaluation runs. We continually test models on a wide range of tasks prior to releasing them. We use many different evaluations (standardized sets of tasks, scored the same way each time), each of which helps to paint a picture of Claude's skills in a particular area. Many of the evaluations we use are public; they are written by outside researchers and can be run by any developer, allowing us to compare capabilities across models. Other evaluations we build in-house.

Because language models are non-deterministic---that is, their responses always involve some element of randomness, and they may carry out the same task slightly differently each time---we have Claude complete each evaluation task hundreds or thousands of times (each attempt is called a run). Testing so many times allows us to understand how a model typically performs, and also to catch rare cases where a model does something we don't expect. What we learn from evaluations shapes decisions across Anthropic, including how we train models, what safeguards we build around them, and when we release them.

Evaluations are also where a model's behavioral issues are sometimes first revealed. Models learn much of what they can do through RL, in which they attempt a task within a specific environment many times over and are rewarded when they succeed. However, training environments are imperfect. If training rewards something we didn't intend---such as finding loopholes or working around a restriction---the model learns that the workaround pays off and may then apply it elsewhere. This is known as reward hacking. While we have processes in place to identify and filter out reward hacking during training, evaluations are a critical mechanism for understanding a model's behavioral propensities in different contexts and on different sets of tasks than those we have in training.

Some tasks---such as searching the web for hard-to-find information---are difficult to realistically simulate in an environment without internet access. Running them with access has been standard practice within the industry: public web search benchmarks are run on the live internet by default, and running them the same way allows us to compare our models with other models. Most of the cases in this report occurred during such evaluations.

Overview of behaviors
---------------------

Below, we describe four categories of behavior in which Claude acted on real websites and systems in ways we did not intend, each of which involved an organization or person outside Anthropic.

### Exploiting a basic flaw in software to run commands on a server

When Claude could not complete an evaluation task directly, either because its own tools were deliberately limited or because an outside service it needed was unavailable, it used other tools hosted on a third party's site to achieve its goal. In some circumstances, it did this by exploiting basic flaws in that site's software, using SQL or command injection (a way of sending input that the site mistakenly runs as instructions).

For example, one evaluation asked Claude Mythos Preview to run a scientific analysis. The public tool it needed to perform that analysis was hosted by a university; when the model sought to access it, the tool returned an error. Looking for another way to complete the task, Claude explored the tool's website, found a script on the university's server that would return any file it was asked for, and used it to copy files from the server, including the script's own code. In that code Claude found the injection flaw that let it run commands on the server, and used it to run the calculation.

In another instance, the data Claude Mythos 5 needed was free, but Claude could not access it without accepting a data use agreement, which it did not have the tools to do. Claude used applications hosted on the website to load the page and accept the agreement on its behalf.

We saw this behavior on DeepSearchQA and BrowseComp (both public web research evaluations), on LABBench2 (a public biology research benchmark), and during internal evaluations.

### Submitting a form it should not have

We saw instances where Claude submitted an online form when it shouldn't have. Generally, this occurred when an evaluation's instructions were ambiguous, or when a misconfiguration within the environment prevented Claude from working with dummy forms.

For example, in a case that happened multiple times on the same evaluation, an unreleased, non-frontier research model was meant to fill out a practice copy of a government form. When the copy failed to load or the model closed it by mistake, the model instead navigated to the website where the real form is normally hosted and submitted the form there.

In another evaluation, Claude Haiku 4.5 was instructed to complete a form up until the final submission stage, but to stop before actually submitting. Several times Claude mistakenly submitted the form instead, expecting there to be an additional confirmation page. In these instances, the model's chain-of-thought stated that it was demonstrating the process, not submitting a real request.

In a third example of this behavior, Claude Haiku 4.5 had been tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages. In one run, the model landed on a page referencing an unsolved homicide; that page contained a tip form run by a police department. Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions. Claude filled out the form with the following: "I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." (The website did not include a description of the perpetrator.) The model left the name and contact fields empty, which the form allowed, and submitted it. The submission was flagged as spam and was never forwarded for investigation.

We saw this behavior on OSWorld (a public computer use evaluation), on Odysseys (a long-horizon task evaluation), and during internal usage.

### Working around restrictions to reach gated data

Claude sometimes worked around a restriction to reach data to which it did not have access. Generally, this occurred when a server refused Claude's request, or when the data was offered only for a fee.

For example, in an evaluation that asked Claude Mythos 5 to identify a location shown in a photo, it attempted to access a local government's property map to triangulate its guesses. Claude could read webpage text, but the evaluation limited its ability to click through it as a person would. Instead, it read the settings file the site sends to browsers, found working access tokens, and used them to send requests directly to the server behind the map to access the data.

In another example of this behavior, an Anthropic researcher used Claude Mythos 5 on a statistics project that required it to pull public data that was available from a state agency for a fee. Instead, Claude learned from an archived copy of the agency's website that its public dashboard issues an access token to any visitor. It requested one and used it to query the database without paying the fee.

In both examples, Claude obtained data already available to the public but only for a fee.

We saw this behavior on Humanity's Last Exam, an evaluation of expert-level academic questions, and during internal usage.

### Using URL shortening services

Some of our fetch tools, which let Claude read webpages, limit the length of the URLs Claude can request. This limit is in place to reduce the risk from Claude using long URLs to take certain unwanted actions, such as exfiltrating larger amounts of data. We saw several models, including Claude Opus 5 and Claude Mythos 5, get around this limitation by using free URL shortening services. We first identified this behavior internally, but as we were writing this post, an operator of the da.gd URL shortening service let us know that they had also found Claude using their website for this purpose. We thank the operator for sharing these details.

Remediation
-----------

We've taken several preventive measures. Some of the public evaluations we no longer run; others we have moved to their offline versions, or rebuilt them so that their tasks do not reach live websites. We've also made broader changes. We have updated the guardrails on some of our internet access tools, such as the web fetch tool, to heavily restrict what the model can do with them. And, as part of our ongoing [agent security and monitoring efforts](https://www.anthropic.com/news/improving-alignment-security-efforts), we have built tooling to automatically detect and block the kinds of behaviors described above. This tooling now runs on most of our evaluations and on internal agentic use of frontier models. When we tested it against the cases described in this post, it blocked all of them.

As we described in our August 31 [post](https://www.anthropic.com/news/improving-alignment-security-efforts), we are also continuing to fix or remove training environments that reward Claude for working around tool restrictions or other blockers, so that they do not incentivize these behaviors or permit reward hacking.

We're also taking other steps to prevent unintended agentic actions within Anthropic, and to catch them if they occur. These include migrating internal agents to centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment, minimizing internet access for internal agents and training processes, and monitoring far more of what agents do through techniques like [safety classifiers](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/cheap-monitors/) and [hierarchical summarization](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/summarization-for-monitoring/). These measures are now part of our security team's detection and response procedures so that we can respond to and contain undesired behavior quickly. We expect to publish more on these approaches, and to build them directly into our products.

Discussion and alignment takeaways
----------------------------------

While we have not completed a full alignment assessment of these cases, we consider them to be less severe than the cybersecurity incidents from this summer. We explain why below, and share the general lessons we've drawn from them.

### Alignment context

As we establish a regular public reporting process for behaviors like these, we also want to situate them in terms of their severity. This remains challenging: judging the extent of an alignment failure often depends on what the model was trying to do, and a model's own account of its reasoning is not necessarily reliable evidence of its beliefs or reasons for action, as we discussed in our September 9 [alignment assessment](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents). As models grow more capable, they can interact with the world in more sophisticated ways, which makes more complex failures possible. For example, the biased reasoning we described in that assessment was not new, but it led to more serious consequences in a setting where models could capably act on real systems for hours at a time. An alignment severity framework built around today's failures could become outdated quickly, given how fast AI capabilities are advancing.

Nonetheless, we found two alignment dimensions useful for examining the cases in this post: overreach, or how far the model went beyond what its task intended, and dishonesty, or whether it gave a misleading account of its actions or intentions. On overreach, we consider these cases to be substantially less concerning than the incidents we reported this summer, in which Claude gained access to real third-party systems for hours during cybersecurity evaluations. In the cases we report here, in contrast, Claude bypassed access controls to reach gated but publicly available data, or exploited software flaws and ran commands on servers (mainly to reach non-sensitive data).

On dishonesty, the comparison is more mixed. In one case, tasked with generating example interactions with websites, Claude submitted an invented tip through a police department's online form. From the transcript, Claude appears to have only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal. In the most serious [incident from this summer,](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents) by contrast, Claude's misleading reasoning was sustained over hours and supported its continued attack. Still, judging dishonesty with confidence typically requires a deeper assessment than we have done here, such as replaying transcripts with modifications to test what drove the model's behavior, so our view of these cases may change with further analysis.

### Lessons and next steps

None of the behaviors we've described here are new, and they do not change our overall view of Claude's alignment. In many of the cases where we observed these behaviors, Claude had been given tasks that were ambiguous or impossible to complete. We and others have observed that when models are given impossible-to-complete tasks, they will pursue unintended and sometimes misaligned strategies to achieve their goals.

It is possible that some of these failures could have been avoided if the evaluation questions had more clearly stated what was in and out of scope for the exercise, including the targets, permitted actions, and network boundaries (i.e., what the model should and shouldn't access). However, Claude encounters ambiguous and impossible tasks every day in real use, and, indeed, several of the cases we observed occurred during regular agentic use of Claude.

Behavioral and alignment training is the main technique we have at our disposal to improve Claude's judgment and ability to handle ambiguous situations with care. Historically, we have been more focused on teaching models to respect boundaries and be appropriately cautious in coding environments. We are now expanding these environments to applications like search and computer use, which were involved in the cases described here. However, alignment training is not yet sufficient or fully robust on its own, at least in the short term, so we also rely on defense-in-depth approaches, including the classifiers and safeguards described above.

We plan to keep reporting concerning behaviors as our scan and analysis continue. We hope these reports help other developers check for similar behaviors in their own models, since many of the evaluations involved are public and widely used. While these cases had minimal impact, we do not want to diminish the findings, because the same behaviors could do far more harm as models become more powerful. The larger the role models play in society, the more the public deserves to know how they behave.

*Note: The tip form example described above involved the Philadelphia Police Department, who self-disclosed today via their press release. We shared this finding with the department on October 8 as soon as our technical review was complete.*

*Corrected Oct 12, 2026:* A previous version of this post incorrectly stated that Claude's web fetch limits were put in place to prevent SQL or command injections. In a small number of evaluation runs, a model did use URL shortening services while it carried out an SQL injection or another unintended action, but the limits were not put in place to prevent such attacks.

PHILADELPHIA (WPVI) -- An Anthropic A.I. model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder through a publicly accessible web form, Philadelphia police said Friday.

The tip was sent through [PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com](https://www.phillyunsolvedmurders.com/) back on July 18, but was flagged as spam and never acted upon.

The department says there has been no indication of unauthorized access to police systems or compromise of department data.

Police say Anthropic discovered the incident on Sept. 28 and notified the department on Oct. 7. A meeting between Anthropic and police officials happened the next day.

"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable," the department said in a statement.

"It should have been detected earlier," said Venkat Margapuri, a computing sciences assistant professor at Villanova University.

Anthropic says it testing how its model interacts with randomly selected websites.

"We don't know exactly what the goal is because just interacting with different websites isn't malicious," said Margapuri.

However, Margapuri says this poses a problem.

"The AI was actively submitting information to a different website on behalf of a user, so that is what I would classify as a high-risk action," said Margapuri.

After the incident, Anthropic told Philadelphia police it ended that testing process and will implement additional authorization in the future in hopes of preventing AI errors.

"It obviously has its own merits, but then it comes with I don't want to say demerits, but it comes with a bunch of risks we should be actively aware of and manage," said Margapuri.

Anthropic [published a report](https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions) about this and other instances of unintended model behavior late Friday stating its agents accessed several federal, state and local government websites.

Anthropic says it notified the White House and each agency involved. The company believes the incidents detailed today had minimal real- world impacts and were not as serious as previous breaches.

Here is the full statement from Philadelphia police:

*The Philadelphia Police Department is informing the public about a false homicide tip submitted by an Anthropic artificial intelligence model through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com.*

*Anthropic notified PPD of the incident on October 7, and department personnel immediately sought to meet with company representatives, which happened on October 8.*

*Anthropic has advised that it plans to publish a report describing this incident and other instances of unintended model behavior today.*

*Philadelphia Police are providing this information to the public ahead of that publication in the interests of full government transparency and accountability.*

*The AI submission was made through the Department's public tip form.*

*Based on the information available and PPD's review, there is no indication that this incident involved any unauthorized access to police systems or a compromise of department data.*

*The submission was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination.*

*PPD is coordinating with the City's Law Department, Office of Innovation and Technology, and Mayor Cherelle L. Parker's executive team.*

*Based on the information reviewed to date, the department's findings are consistent with Anthropic's account of how the submission interacted with the website.*

*According to Anthropic, its model was conducting a test involving interactions with randomly selected websites when it accessed PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com and submitted false information concerning an unsolved homicide.*

*The submission, dated July 18, 2026, at 11:27 p.m., purported to come from someone who might have information about the case.*

*Anthropic told PPD that it discovered the incident on September 28, terminated the automated testing process responsible for the submission and instituted an additional validation mechanism for future testing.*

*Following the October 8 briefing, PPD located the submission in the website's tip records and confirmed that the corresponding email remained in spam.*

*The department's regular investigative process for crime tips requires human review and vetting before any tips are disseminated for investigative follow-up.*

*Regardless of who submits information or how it reaches the department, a tip is a lead to assess - not an established fact.*

*Investigators evaluate its credibility and seek corroborating evidence. An automated submission does not bypass that process.*

*Those PPD safeguards limited the impact of this incident. They do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide.*

*Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers.*

*Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.*

*PPD will review Anthropic's published report and any additional information relevant to its systems or investigations. The City of Philadelphia takes this incident very seriously.*

*The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable.*

*Members of the public should continue to submit legitimate information about unsolved homicides through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com.*

*PPD remains committed to carefully evaluating that information and pursuing credible leads on behalf of victims and their families.*

*The department and the Parker administration will continue to closely monitor this incident, and will provide more information to the public as soon as it becomes available.*

*In addition to our investigation into this incident, the Parker administration will explore all necessary regulatory protections going forward locally along with our state and federal partners.*

*The City of Philadelphia under Mayor Parker's leadership is adopting AI responsibly, and is committed to transparency, careful implementation, and safeguards that reduce errors and protect City systems and residents.*
reports_full.title: AI model submitted false tip about unsolved murder, Philadelphia police say

reports_full.text:
Rogue AI models have hacked companies and tried to break into government websites. Now one has submitted a fake tip for an unsolved crime.

Police in [Philadelphia](https://www.wsj.com/topics/place/philadelphia) say Anthropic alerted them this week that one of its artificial-intelligence models submitted a false homicide tip through [PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com](http://phillyunsolvedmurders.com/).

In a blog post, Anthropic said the fake tip was among a group of rogue actions the company uncovered recently. The rogue activity also involved websites run by U.S. government agencies at the federal, state and local levels. The company said it has briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved, and plans to report new instances of unintended AI behavior as it uncovers them.

"While these cases had minimal impact, we do not want to diminish the findings, because the same behaviors could do far more harm as models become more powerful," Anthropic said in the blog post.

The false-report incident happened in July. Anthropic didn't realize it until September.

"The City of Philadelphia takes this incident very seriously," the police department said on Friday. "The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."

Anthropic's model was conducting a test involving interactions with randomly selected websites when it submitted the tip pretending to be someone who might have information about an unsolved case, police said. 

The submission, dated July 18, went to spam and was never sent for further investigation. That doesn't take away from the seriousness of what happened, police said. 

"Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers," the department said. "Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement."

Anthropic told the Philadelphia police that the company discovered the incident on Sept. 28, and terminated the automated testing process responsible for the submission, the department said. Anthropic also told the police it added an additional validation mechanism for future testing, according to the agency. 

Anthropic notified the Philadelphia police on Oct. 7, nine days after discovering the incident. Police said the company met with the department the next day.

Anthropic said it identified most of the cases disclosed Friday in a review of transcripts that the company began in July.

Multiple times, the company said, an unreleased model was directed to fill out a practice copy of a government form but navigated to the website where the real form was hosted and submitted the form.

The false murder tip originated when the model encountered a tip form run by a police department on a page referencing an unsolved homicide. The company said Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases or submit anything destructive, but said the instructions didn't rule out form submissions.

Claude entered: "I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." Anthropic said Claude left the name and contact fields empty.

Anthropic said it has built tools to automatically detect and block these kinds of behaviors.

Anthropic has previously alerted police departments to more substantive information about potential risks. In late September, the sheriff's office in Florida's Lee County arrested a woman after a tip from Anthropic. The woman had made statements that she would "shoot up" the county's sheriff's office, according to the arrest report.

AI companies haven't always alerted law enforcement to potential risks. In February, Canadian law enforcement named Jesse Van Rootselaar as the suspect in the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting, months after [OpenAI](https://www.wsj.com/topics/subject/openai) employees had considered alerting law enforcement about Van Rootselaar's interactions with the [company's chatbot](https://www.wsj.com/us-news/law/openai-employees-raised-alarms-about-canada-shooting-suspect-months-ago-b585df62?mod=article_inline). [OpenAI](https://www.wsj.com/topics/subject/openai) ultimately decided [not to contact authorities](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/british-columbia-sues-openai-alleging-chatgpt-aided-mass-school-shooting-aac66568?mod=article_inline), and the company now [faces a lawsuit](https://www.wsj.com/us-news/law/openai-lawsuits-mount-over-canadian-school-shooting-ca24c762?mod=article_inline) from British Columbia as well as dozens of victims.

PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, where the fake tip was sent in, is a Philadelphia police website that lists unsolved homicides, takes tips on cases and offers a $20,000 reward for information that leads to an arrest.

"Members of the public should continue to submit legitimate information about unsolved homicides through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com," the police said.
reports_full.title: Anthropic AI Model Went Rogue, Submitted Fake Unsolved Murder Tip

reports_full.text:
SAN FRANCISCO --- Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, said that some of its AI agents had taken unintended actions on federal, state and local websites, including submitting a false tip about a murder to a Philadelphia [police hotline](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/09/ai-system-submits-false-homicide-tip-philadelphia-police/ "https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/09/ai-system-submits-false-homicide-tip-philadelphia-police/").

The State Department said separately Friday that an Anthropic testing model had filed 19 visa applications in August and another in May using a form on the department's website.

Anthropic said in a report published Friday that an internal review had discovered that its AI models had acted inappropriately in some instances during testing and while employees were using them.

In one incident, an AI agent exploited a design flaw in a state government website to freely access public data that usually required paying a fee. In another incident, an AI agent submitted a federal government form when it was instructed not to.

"We have briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved," Anthropic wrote in its report. The company said the incidents led it to turn off internet access for AI agents during all internal testing, pending a review of security measures.

The State Department said in a statement that the visa applications were incomplete and not processed.

"At no time were any of the Department's systems compromised or hacked by the Anthropic model," the department said.

The incidents revealed Friday are the latest in a growing number of disclosures from leading AI companies about their models hacking into websites, going beyond their explicit instructions or acting in ways they weren't intended to online.

Anthropic did not disclose in the report how many incidents it found, and a spokesperson for the company did not return a request for comment asking for more details.

The latest AI agents are trained to be persistent in attempting to complete their tasks to make them more effective. But the industry is struggling to ensure that the technology doesn't, in the process, cross into unethical or illegal behavior.

Anthropic said in its report that the newly disclosed incidents were not as concerning as those it [reported earlier this summer](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/07/30/anthropic-discloses-that-ai-models-testing-hacked-three-companies/ "https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/07/30/anthropic-discloses-that-ai-models-testing-hacked-three-companies/"), in which one agent hacked into another company's website and another tried to convince a human engineer to approve malicious code for an open source software project. OpenAI, Google and Meta all also reported incidents of their AI agents hacking into other companies.

But Anthropic said the latest examples included instances of its AI exploiting "basic flaws" in websites, using common hacking techniques.

Anthropic released the report disclosing the new incidents on Friday, hours after the Philadelphia Police Department [criticized the company](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/09/ai-system-submits-false-homicide-tip-philadelphia-police/ "https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/09/ai-system-submits-false-homicide-tip-philadelphia-police/") for not informing it earlier about the incident in which the AI agent submitted the false murder tip.

That incident occurred when agents were tasked with interacting with random websites during a testing run, Anthropic said. One agent filled out the tip form and submitted it, writing, "I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant," according to Anthropic's report.

The company's disclosures don't go far enough, said Sydney Von Arx, chief executive of AI safety organization Nightingale Collective, who is part of a community of [independent researchers](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/02/independent-researchers-are-revealing-new-details-about-rogue-ai-agents/ "https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/02/independent-researchers-are-revealing-new-details-about-rogue-ai-agents/") investigating AI agent mishaps that has revealed undisclosed incidents to the public.

"They should be doing more of a deep-dive into how this went on for so long without them noticing and stopping it," Von Arx said. "At a bare minimum, Anthropic should share how many times their models have taken actions that would be felonies if a human did them."

Anthropic wrote in its report that the company was not disclosing the names of the governments or agencies that had their websites impacted, because it didn't want to expose potential vulnerabilities.

The company's decision to shut off its AI agents from the internet during internal tests builds on precautions introduced earlier this year. After the incidents in which its technology hacked into other organizations, Anthropic said it had turned off internet access for "high risk" and cybersecurity testing.

*Ian Duncan contributed to this article.*
